title: Short Stuff: How Eyes In a Painting Follow You
summary: Short Stuff episode explaining why the eyes in a painting seem to follow a viewer around the room. The hosts tie it to the earlier Mona Lisa discussion and cover linear perspective, which Filippo Brunelleschi stumbled onto in Italy; depth cues from light and shadow; why painting eyes that gaze straight out is hard (the roughly nine-degree sweet spot); why real people and sculptures don't produce the effect when you move around them; and a 2004 study using a digitally rendered mannequin torso image to show the effect is real perception, not a trick of the viewer.
topics: eyes in a painting follow you

segments.title: Opening and setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic as a follow-up to an earlier Mona Lisa episode and say the eyes-following effect is easy to understand but hard to explain.
topics: eyes in a painting follow you

segments.title: Linear perspective and Brunelleschi
segments.summary: Linear perspective is described as lines in a painting converging to a single point, credited to the Italian architect Filippo Brunelleschi, who worked on the Baptistery in Florence. Earlier flat art, such as Egyptian painting, relied on size alone to show distance.

segments.title: Light, shadow, and illusion of depth
segments.summary: Light and shadow are described as additional ways to suggest a third dimension on a flat surface, which is an optical illusion.

segments.title: Difficulty of painting eyes that meet the viewer
segments.summary: The hosts explain that painting eyes that look at the viewer is very hard, and that a head turned about nine degrees from the canvas makes it easier, while tilted heads make it harder because of how much white and iris show.

segments.title: Why real people and statues don't do this
segments.summary: Moving around a live person or a sculpture changes your perspective and gives your brain new visual cues, so their eyes do not appear to follow you. A painting's depth cues are fixed, so its gaze stays the same from any angle.
topics: eyes in a painting follow you

segments.title: 2004 mannequin study and gaze illusion
segments.summary: A 2004 study by researchers used a digitally rendered image of a mannequin torso to show that the eyes-following effect is how the viewer perceives the image, not an error on the viewer's part. The hosts also say a painted gaze that is off to the side creates a sense of looking into the distance.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts recap that painted eyes look the same from any angle, so they seem to follow the viewer, and close the episode.
